metadata.chapter_name: THE HUMAN EYE AND THE COLOURFUL WORLD

chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The eye enables us to see the wonderful world and colours; it is the most significant sense organ because it lets us see the colourful world.
We cannot identify colours with closed eyes, though smell, taste, sound and touch can identify objects to some extent.
The eye lens system forms an image on the RETINA, which is a delicate light-sensitive membrane.
LIGHT enters the eye through the CORNEA, a thin transparent membrane forming the front bulge of the eyeball.
This chapter uses ideas of refraction of light by lenses (from Chapter 9) to study optical phenomena in nature.

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: DEFINITION: The human eye is a valuable sense organ that works like a camera. Its lens system forms an inverted real image of the object on the RETINA, a light-sensitive screen. The eyeball is approximately spherical with a diameter of about 2.3 cm.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: LIGHT enters the eye through a thin membrane called the CORNEA, which forms the transparent bulge on the front surface of the eyeball.
Most of the refraction of light rays entering the eye occurs at the OUTER SURFACE OF THE CORNEA.
The CRYSTALLINE LENS merely provides the finer adjustment of focal length to focus objects at different distances on the retina.
The IRIS is a dark muscular diaphragm behind the cornea that controls the size of the PUPIL.
The PUPIL regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye.
The eye lens forms an INVERTED REAL IMAGE of the object on the retina.
The RETINA is a delicate membrane having an enormous number of LIGHT-SENSITIVE CELLS. These cells get activated upon illumination and generate ELECTRICAL SIGNALS.
The electrical signals are sent to the brain via the OPTIC NERVES. The brain interprets these signals and processes the information so that we perceive objects as they are.

items.question: What is the function of the iris and the pupil in the human eye?
items.answer: The IRIS is a dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the PUPIL. The PUPIL regulates and controls the amount of LIGHT entering the eye.

items.question: Through which part does light enter the eye, and where is the image finally formed?
items.answer: Light enters the eye through a thin transparent membrane called the CORNEA. The image is finally formed on the RETINA, a light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye.

items.question: Explain how the retina helps us to see an object.
items.answer: The RETINA is a delicate membrane with an enormous number of LIGHT-SENSITIVE CELLS. When light falls on it, these cells get activated and generate ELECTRICAL SIGNALS. These signals are sent to the brain through the OPTIC NERVES, and the brain interprets them so that we perceive the object as it is.

items.question: Describe the path of light through the human eye until an image is formed.
items.answer: Light first enters the eye through the CORNEA, where most of the refraction takes place at its outer surface. It then passes through the PUPIL, whose size is controlled by the IRIS to regulate the amount of light. The CRYSTALLINE LENS gives the finer focal-length adjustment and forms an INVERTED REAL IMAGE of the object on the RETINA. The light-sensitive cells of the retina generate electrical signals carried by the optic nerves to the brain.

items.question: Why is the human eye compared to a camera? Give the main points of comparison.
items.answer: The human eye is compared to a CAMERA because both use a lens system to form an image on a light-sensitive surface. In a camera the image forms on the film or sensor, while in the eye it forms on the RETINA. In both, an INVERTED REAL IMAGE is formed, and the amount of light is controlled by an opening (the diaphragm in a camera and the PUPIL controlled by the iris in the eye).

items.question: Describe the structure of the human eye and explain the function of its main parts.
items.answer:
The human eye is approximately spherical with a diameter of about 2.3 cm.
(i) CORNEA: A thin transparent membrane forming the front bulge of the eyeball; most refraction of entering light occurs at its outer surface.
(ii) IRIS: A dark muscular diaphragm behind the cornea that controls the size of the pupil.
(iii) PUPIL: The central opening that regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye.
(iv) CRYSTALLINE LENS: Provides the finer adjustment of focal length to focus objects at different distances on the retina; it forms an inverted real image.
(v) RETINA: A delicate light-sensitive membrane at the back of the eye whose cells generate electrical signals when illuminated.
(vi) OPTIC NERVE: Carries these electrical signals to the brain, which interprets them so we perceive objects as they are.

items.question: On which part of the eye is the image of an object formed?
items.answer: D
items.explanation: The eye lens forms an inverted real image on the retina. The cornea, iris and pupil are involved in admitting and refracting light, not in receiving the image.

items.question: Which part of the eye controls the amount of light entering it?
items.answer: A
items.explanation: The pupil regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye, with its size controlled by the iris. The other parts do not control light entry.

items.question: Most of the refraction of light entering the eye occurs at the
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Most refraction takes place at the outer surface of the cornea; the crystalline lens only provides finer focal-length adjustment.

items.question: The electrical signals generated by the retina are carried to the brain by the
items.answer: C
items.explanation: The light-sensitive cells of the retina generate electrical signals that are sent to the brain through the optic nerves; the other parts have different functions.

items.question: The approximate diameter of the human eyeball is
items.answer: B
items.explanation: The eyeball is approximately spherical with a diameter of about 2.3 cm, as stated in the textbook.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The eye lens is composed of a fibrous, JELLY-LIKE material whose curvature can be modified by the CILIARY MUSCLES.
When the ciliary muscles are RELAXED, the lens becomes THIN, its focal length INCREASES, and we can see distant objects clearly.
When the ciliary muscles CONTRACT, the curvature of the eye lens increases, the lens becomes THICKER, its focal length DECREASES, and we can see nearby objects clearly.
The focal length of the eye lens CANNOT be decreased below a certain minimum limit; an object held too close appears blurred.
NEAR POINT (least distance of distinct vision): the minimum distance at which objects can be seen most distinctly without strain. For a young adult with normal vision it is about 25 cm.
FAR POINT: the farthest point up to which the eye can see objects clearly. For a normal eye it is INFINITY.
A normal eye can see objects clearly between 25 cm and infinity.
CATARACT: Sometimes the crystalline lens of people of old age becomes milky and cloudy, causing partial or complete loss of vision. Vision can be restored through cataract surgery.

items.question: What is meant by the power of accommodation of the eye?
items.answer: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its FOCAL LENGTH (by changing its curvature) so as to focus objects at different distances clearly on the retina is called the POWER OF ACCOMMODATION.

items.question: What is the near point and the far point of a normal human eye?
items.answer: The NEAR POINT is the minimum distance at which an object can be seen most distinctly without strain, about 25 cm for a normal eye. The FAR POINT is the farthest distance up to which the eye can see clearly, which is INFINITY for a normal eye.

items.question: How do the ciliary muscles help in the accommodation of the eye?
items.answer: The CILIARY MUSCLES modify the curvature of the eye lens. When they are RELAXED, the lens becomes thin and its focal length increases, allowing distant objects to be seen clearly. When they CONTRACT, the curvature increases, the lens becomes thicker and its focal length decreases, allowing nearby objects to be seen clearly.

items.question: Why is a normal eye not able to see clearly the objects placed closer than 25 cm?
items.answer: To see a nearby object clearly, the eye lens must increase its curvature and decrease its focal length. However, the focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a certain MINIMUM LIMIT. For an object placed closer than 25 cm (the near point), the lens cannot reduce its focal length enough to form a sharp image on the retina, so the object appears blurred and the eye feels strained.

items.question: Explain how the focal length of the eye lens changes when we look at a distant object and then at a nearby object.
items.answer: When looking at a DISTANT object, the ciliary muscles RELAX, the eye lens becomes THIN, and its focal length INCREASES so that the distant object is focused on the retina. When looking at a NEARBY object, the ciliary muscles CONTRACT, increasing the curvature of the lens; the lens becomes THICKER and its focal length DECREASES so that the nearby object is focused on the retina.

items.question: Define accommodation. Explain how the eye sees both near and distant objects clearly, and state what cataract is.
items.answer:
ACCOMMODATION is the ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length to focus objects at different distances on the retina.
- For DISTANT objects: the ciliary muscles relax, the lens becomes thin, focal length increases, and the image forms on the retina.
- For NEARBY objects: the ciliary muscles contract, the curvature of the lens increases, the lens becomes thicker, focal length decreases, and the image forms on the retina.
- The focal length cannot be reduced below a minimum limit, so objects closer than the near point (about 25 cm) cannot be seen clearly.
- CATARACT: In old age the crystalline lens may become milky and cloudy, causing partial or complete loss of vision. It can be treated by cataract surgery to restore vision.

items.question: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length is called
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Accommodation is defined as the eye lens adjusting its focal length to focus objects at different distances. The other terms refer to different optical phenomena.

items.question: The least distance of distinct vision for a young adult with normal eyes is about
items.answer: C
items.explanation: The near point (least distance of distinct vision) for a normal eye is about 25 cm; the other values are incorrect.

items.question: When the ciliary muscles are relaxed, the eye lens becomes

options.A: thin with a larger focal length.
options.B: thick with a smaller focal length.
options.C: thin with a smaller focal length.
options.D: thick with a larger focal length.

items.answer: A
items.explanation: Relaxed ciliary muscles make the lens thin, increasing its focal length so distant objects are seen clearly. The other combinations are wrong.

items.question: The change in the focal length of the eye lens is caused by the action of the
items.answer: C
items.explanation: The ciliary muscles modify the curvature of the lens, changing its focal length. The iris controls the pupil, and the retina receives the image.

items.question: The far point of a normal human eye is
items.answer: C
items.explanation: A normal eye can see objects clearly up to infinity, so its far point is infinity; 25 cm is the near point.

items.question: The clouding of the crystalline lens in old age, causing loss of vision, is called
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Cataract is the milky, cloudy condition of the lens in old age, treatable by surgery. Myopia, presbyopia and hypermetropia are refractive defects.

topics.topic_name: DEFECTS OF VISION AND THEIR CORRECTION

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: MYOPIA (Near-sightedness): A person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly. The far point is nearer than infinity.
Cause: (i) excessive curvature of the eye lens, or (ii) elongation of the eyeball.
In a myopic eye, the image of a distant object forms IN FRONT OF the retina.
Correction: a CONCAVE lens of suitable power brings the image back onto the retina.
HYPERMETROPIA (Far-sightedness): A person can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly. The near point is FARTHER away than the normal near point (25 cm).
Cause: (i) the focal length of the eye lens is too long, or (ii) the eyeball has become too small.
In a hypermetropic eye, the image of a nearby object forms BEHIND the retina.
Correction: a CONVEX lens of appropriate power provides the additional focussing power to form the image on the retina.

PRESBYOPIA: The power of accommodation of the eye usually decreases with AGEING; the near point gradually recedes away, and the person finds it difficult to see nearby objects clearly without corrective glasses.
Cause: weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens.
A person may suffer from both myopia and hypermetropia, requiring BI-FOCAL lenses (upper concave part for distant vision, lower convex part for near vision).
These days refractive defects can also be corrected with CONTACT LENSES or through surgical interventions.

(b) Myopic eye - the image of the distant object forms in front of the retina.

(b) Hypermetropic eye - the image of a nearby object forms behind the retina.
(c) Correction for hypermetropia - a convex lens placed before the eye converges the rays so that the image forms on the retina.
(Labels: N = near point of a hypermetropic eye; N' = near point of a normal eye.)

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS:
sections.text:
[THINK IT OVER box - Eye Donation]
- Our eyes can live even after our death. By donating our eyes after we die, we can light the life of a blind person.
- About 35 million people in the developing world are blind, and most of them can be cured. About 4.5 million people with CORNEAL BLINDNESS can be cured through corneal transplantation of donated eyes. Out of these 4.5 million, 60% are children below the age of 12.
- Things to keep in mind when eyes are to be donated:
- Eye donors can belong to any age group or sex. People who use spectacles, or those operated for cataract, can still donate the eyes. People who are diabetic, have hypertension, asthma patients and those without communicable diseases can also donate eyes.
- Eyes must be removed within 4-6 hours after death. Inform the nearest eye bank immediately.
- The eye bank team will remove the eyes at the home of the deceased or at a hospital.
- Eye removal takes only 10-15 minutes. It is a simple process and does not lead to any disfigurement.
- Persons who were infected with or died because of AIDS, Hepatitis B or C, rabies, acute leukaemia, tetanus, cholera, meningitis or encephalitis cannot donate eyes.
- An eye bank collects, evaluates and distributes the donated eyes. All eyes donated are evaluated using strict medical standards. Eyes found unsuitable for transplantation are used for valuable research and medical education. The identities of both the donor and the recipient remain confidential.
- One pair of eyes gives vision to up to FOUR corneal blind people.
- (Accompanying verse by C. Cibber): "You talk of wondrous things you see, / You say the sun shines bright; / I feel him warm, but how can he / Or make it day or night?"

items.question: What is myopia and how is it corrected?
items.answer: MYOPIA (near-sightedness) is a defect in which a person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly because the image forms in front of the retina. It is corrected using a CONCAVE lens of suitable power.

items.question: What is hypermetropia and which lens is used to correct it?
items.answer: HYPERMETROPIA (far-sightedness) is a defect in which a person can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly because the image forms behind the retina. It is corrected using a CONVEX lens of appropriate power.

items.question: State the causes of myopia and how the image is formed in a myopic eye.
items.answer: Myopia arises due to (i) EXCESSIVE CURVATURE of the eye lens, or (ii) ELONGATION of the eyeball. Because of this, the image of a distant object is formed IN FRONT OF the retina instead of on it, so distant objects appear blurred.

items.question: Explain presbyopia, its cause and its correction.
items.answer: PRESBYOPIA is a defect in which the power of accommodation of the eye decreases with AGEING, so the near point gradually recedes and the person cannot see nearby objects clearly without glasses. It is caused by the WEAKENING of the ciliary muscles and the DIMINISHING FLEXIBILITY of the eye lens. It is corrected using a convex lens; if the person also has myopia, BI-FOCAL lenses (concave upper part for distance, convex lower part for reading) are used.

items.question: Why does a hypermetropic person need a convex lens? Explain with the position of the image.
items.answer: In a HYPERMETROPIC eye, either the focal length of the eye lens is too long or the eyeball is too small, so the image of a nearby object is formed BEHIND the retina and the object appears blurred. A CONVEX lens of appropriate power provides the additional converging (focussing) power needed to bring the image forward onto the retina, allowing nearby objects to be seen clearly.

items.question: Describe the three common refractive defects of vision along with their causes and corrections.
items.answer:
(i) MYOPIA (near-sightedness): Distant objects are not seen clearly; image forms in front of the retina. Cause: excessive curvature of the lens or elongation of the eyeball. Correction: concave lens.
(ii) HYPERMETROPIA (far-sightedness): Nearby objects are not seen clearly; image forms behind the retina. Cause: too long a focal length of the lens or too small an eyeball. Correction: convex lens.
(iii) PRESBYOPIA: Difficulty seeing nearby objects with ageing as the near point recedes. Cause: weakening of ciliary muscles and reduced flexibility of the lens. Correction: convex lens, or bi-focal lenses if myopia is also present. These defects may also be corrected by contact lenses or surgery.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Myopia can be corrected by using a
items.answer: B
items.explanation: A concave (diverging) lens corrects myopia by moving the image back onto the retina. A convex lens corrects hypermetropia.

items.question: A person who can see distant objects clearly but not nearby objects suffers from
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Hypermetropia (far-sightedness) is the inability to see nearby objects clearly. Myopia is the opposite defect.

items.question: In a myopic eye, the image of a distant object is formed
items.answer: B
items.explanation: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina due to excessive curvature of the lens or an elongated eyeball, so distant objects look blurred.

items.question: The defect of vision in which a person requires bi-focal lenses is usually associated with

options.C: presbyopia with both myopia and hypermetropia.

items.answer: C
items.explanation: A person suffering from both myopia and hypermetropia (often with presbyopia) needs bi-focal lenses having a concave upper part and a convex lower part.

items.question: The main cause of presbyopia is

options.A: excessive curvature of the eye lens.
options.C: weakening of ciliary muscles and reduced flexibility of the eye lens.

items.answer: C
items.explanation: Presbyopia results from weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the lens with age. Clouding of the lens is cataract.

topics.topic_name: REFRACTION OF LIGHT THROUGH A PRISM

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: When light passes through a rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but slightly displaced laterally.
A prism has two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral surfaces inclined to each other.
The angle between the two lateral faces of the prism is the ANGLE OF THE PRISM (angle A).
At the first surface, light enters from air to glass and bends TOWARDS the normal.
At the second surface, light enters from glass to air and bends AWAY FROM the normal.
The peculiar shape of the prism makes the emergent ray bend at an angle to the incident ray; this angle is the ANGLE OF DEVIATION (angle D).

Terms (Figure 10.4): PE = incident ray; EF = refracted ray; FS = emergent ray; angle i = angle of incidence; angle r = angle of refraction; angle e = angle of emergence; angle A = angle of the prism; angle D = angle of deviation.

sections.label: DIAGRAMS IN THIS TOPIC:
sections.raw: - Figure 10.4 (Refraction of light through a triangular glass prism): A triangular prism ABC with apex A at the top and base BC at the bottom. An incident ray PE strikes the face AB at point E (angle of incidence i), refracts towards the normal NN' inside the prism as ray EF, then strikes face AC at point F and refracts away from the normal MM' as the emergent ray FS (angle of emergence e). The original direction of the incident ray and the emergent ray meet at G, and the angle between them is the angle of deviation D. The angle of the prism A is the angle at the apex.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.1:
sections.aim: To study the refraction of light through a triangular glass prism by tracing the path of light.
sections.materials: A sheet of white paper, a drawing board, drawing pins, a triangular glass prism, a pencil, four pins, and a scale.
procedure: 1. Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board using drawing pins.
2. Place a glass prism on it so that it rests on its triangular base. Trace the outline of the prism using a pencil.
3. Draw a straight line PE inclined to one of the refracting surfaces, say AB, of the prism.
4. Fix two pins, say at points P and Q, on the line PE.
5. Look for the images of the pins fixed at P and Q through the other face AC.
6. Fix two more pins at points R and S such that the pins at R and S and the images of the pins at P and Q lie on the same straight line.
7. Remove the pins and the glass prism.
8. The line PE meets the boundary of the prism at point E; join and produce the points R and S so that these lines meet the boundary of the prism at E and F respectively. Join E and F.
9. Draw perpendiculars (normals) to the refracting surfaces AB and AC at points E and F respectively.
10. Mark the angle of incidence (angle i), the angle of refraction (angle r) and the angle of emergence (angle e).
sections.observation: The incident ray PE bends towards the normal at E (entering glass from air), travels as EF inside the prism, and bends away from the normal at F (leaving glass to air) as emergent ray FS. The emergent ray FS travels at an angle to the incident ray PE.
sections.conclusion:
A ray of light passing through a triangular glass prism bends towards the base, and the emergent ray is deviated from the direction of the incident ray by the ANGLE OF DEVIATION (angle D).

items.question: What is meant by the angle of the prism and the angle of deviation?
items.answer: The ANGLE OF THE PRISM is the angle between the two lateral (refracting) faces of the prism. The ANGLE OF DEVIATION is the angle between the direction of the incident ray and the emergent ray.

items.question: How does a ray of light bend at the two refracting surfaces of a prism?
items.answer: At the first surface (air to glass) the ray bends TOWARDS the normal. At the second surface (glass to air) the ray bends AWAY FROM the normal.

items.question: How is the refraction of light through a prism different from that through a rectangular glass slab?
items.answer: In a glass SLAB, the two refracting surfaces are parallel, so the emergent ray is PARALLEL to the incident ray and only displaced laterally. In a PRISM, the refracting surfaces are inclined to each other, so the emergent ray is bent at an angle (the ANGLE OF DEVIATION) to the incident ray and is not parallel to it.

items.question: Define the terms angle of incidence, angle of refraction, angle of emergence and angle of deviation with reference to a prism.
items.answer:
With reference to Figure 10.4 of a prism:
- ANGLE OF INCIDENCE (i): the angle between the incident ray PE and the normal at the first surface.
- ANGLE OF REFRACTION (r): the angle between the refracted ray EF and the normal at the first surface.
- ANGLE OF EMERGENCE (e): the angle between the emergent ray FS and the normal at the second surface.
- ANGLE OF DEVIATION (D): the angle between the direction of the incident ray and the emergent ray.

items.question: Describe the path of a light ray as it passes through a triangular glass prism.
items.answer: A light ray PE strikes the first refracting surface AB and, on entering glass from air, bends TOWARDS the normal to become the refracted ray EF inside the prism. The ray EF then strikes the second surface AC and, on leaving glass into air, bends AWAY FROM the normal to become the emergent ray FS. Because the surfaces are inclined, the emergent ray is deviated from the original direction by the ANGLE OF DEVIATION D, with the ray effectively bending towards the base of the prism.

items.question: Explain Activity 10.1 used to trace the path of light through a prism, and state its conclusion.
items.answer:
A glass prism is placed on a sheet of white paper fixed to a drawing board, and its outline is traced. A line PE is drawn inclined to face AB, and two pins are fixed at P and Q on it. Looking through face AC, two more pins R and S are fixed so that they appear in line with the images of P and Q. After removing the pins and prism, the entry point E and exit point F are joined, normals are drawn at E and F, and the angles of incidence (i), refraction (r) and emergence (e) are marked. The experiment shows that the ray bends towards the normal at the first surface and away from the normal at the second surface, and that the emergent ray is deviated from the incident ray by the ANGLE OF DEVIATION, confirming the bending of light through a prism towards its base.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The angle between the two lateral faces of a prism is called the
items.answer: B
items.explanation: The angle between the two refracting (lateral) faces is defined as the angle of the prism. The others refer to ray angles.

items.question: When light passes from air into a glass prism at the first surface, it bends
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Going from a rarer (air) to a denser (glass) medium, light bends towards the normal at the first surface.

items.question: The angle between the direction of the incident ray and the emergent ray of a prism is the
items.answer: C
items.explanation: The angle of deviation is the angle between the incident ray's direction and the emergent ray; the others are defined at the surfaces.

items.question: Unlike a glass slab, the emergent ray from a prism is

options.B: bent at an angle to the incident ray.

items.answer: B
items.explanation: Because the prism faces are inclined, the emergent ray is deviated from the incident ray, whereas in a parallel-faced slab it stays parallel.

items.question: In Figure 10.4, the ray FS represents the
items.answer: C
items.explanation: PE is the incident ray, EF the refracted ray, and FS is the emergent ray leaving the second surface of the prism.

topics.topic_name: DISPERSION OF WHITE LIGHT BY A GLASS PRISM

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A glass prism splits incident white light into a band of colours; the band of coloured components is called its SPECTRUM.
The seven colours of the spectrum are Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red - remembered by VIBGYOR.
Different colours of light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through the prism.
RED light bends the LEAST while VIOLET light bends the MOST. Thus the rays of each colour emerge along different paths and become distinct.

Isaac NEWTON was the first to use a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight. Using a second identical inverted prism, he recombined the colours to get white light again, showing that sunlight is made up of seven colours.
Any light that gives a spectrum similar to that of sunlight is called WHITE LIGHT.
A RAINBOW is a natural spectrum appearing in the sky after a rain shower, caused by dispersion of sunlight by tiny water droplets in the atmosphere.

A rainbow is always formed in a direction OPPOSITE to that of the Sun. The water droplets act like small prisms: they refract and disperse the incident sunlight, reflect it internally, and refract it again as it comes out of the droplet.
A rainbow can also be seen on a sunny day through a waterfall or fountain with the Sun behind the observer.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.2:
sections.aim: To observe the dispersion of white light (sunlight) by a glass prism.
sections.materials: A thick sheet of cardboard, a glass prism, and a nearby screen (white wall/paper); sunlight as the source.
procedure: 1. Take a thick sheet of cardboard and make a small hole or narrow slit in its middle.
2. Allow sunlight to fall on the narrow slit. This gives a narrow beam of white light.
3. Take a glass prism and allow the light from the slit to fall on one of its faces.
4. Turn the prism slowly until the light coming out of it appears on a nearby screen.
sections.observation: A beautiful band of colours (the spectrum) appears on the screen. The colours seen, in sequence, are Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red (VIBGYOR).
sections.conclusion:
White light is composed of seven colours; on passing through a glass prism it splits into its component colours. This splitting of light into its component colours is called DISPERSION.

items.question: What is dispersion of light? Name the seven colours of the spectrum in order.
items.answer: DISPERSION is the splitting of white light into its component colours on passing through a prism. The seven colours in order are Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red (VIBGYOR).

items.question: Which colour of light bends the most and which bends the least on passing through a prism?
items.answer: VIOLET light bends the MOST and RED light bends the LEAST while passing through a glass prism.

items.question: How did Newton show that white light is made up of seven colours?
items.answer: Newton used a glass prism to split sunlight into a spectrum of seven colours. When he placed a second identical prism in an INVERTED position with respect to the first, all the colours of the spectrum passed through it and RECOMBINED into a beam of WHITE LIGHT. This showed that sunlight is made up of seven colours.

items.question: Why do different colours emerge along different paths when white light passes through a prism?
items.answer: Different colours of light bend through DIFFERENT ANGLES with respect to the incident ray as they pass through the prism. RED light bends the least and VIOLET light bends the most, with the other colours bending by intermediate amounts. As a result, the rays of each colour emerge along different paths and become DISTINCT, producing the spectrum.

items.question: Explain how a rainbow is formed in the sky.
items.answer: A rainbow is a natural spectrum formed after a rain shower due to DISPERSION of sunlight by tiny water droplets present in the atmosphere. Each water droplet acts like a small prism. When sunlight enters a droplet, it is refracted and dispersed into its colours; the light is then internally reflected at the back of the droplet and refracted again as it leaves. Due to this dispersion and internal reflection, different colours reach the observer's eye, and the rainbow is always formed in a direction OPPOSITE to the Sun.

items.question: Define dispersion and spectrum. Describe Activity 10.2 to demonstrate dispersion of white light.
items.answer:
DISPERSION is the splitting of white light into its component colours; the band of these coloured components is called the SPECTRUM (VIBGYOR).
Activity 10.2: A thick cardboard sheet with a narrow slit is used to obtain a narrow beam of sunlight (white light). This beam is allowed to fall on one face of a glass prism, and the prism is turned slowly until the emerging light falls on a nearby screen. A beautiful band of seven colours appears on the screen, showing that white light is composed of seven colours and that the prism disperses it into its components. This confirms the phenomenon of dispersion.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Air just above a fire or radiator becomes hotter (less dense) than the cooler air above it, and has a slightly lower refractive index. Since these conditions are not stationary, the apparent position of an object seen through the hot air fluctuates, causing a wavering effect - an example of atmospheric refraction on a small scale.
TWINKLING OF STARS:
The twinkling of a star is due to atmospheric refraction of starlight.
On entering the Earth's atmosphere, starlight undergoes refraction continuously before reaching the Earth, in a medium of gradually changing refractive index.

Since the atmosphere bends starlight towards the normal, the apparent position of the star is slightly different from its actual position; the star appears slightly higher (above) than its actual position when viewed near the horizon.
This apparent position keeps changing slightly because the physical conditions of the atmosphere are not stationary.

Stars are very distant and approximate POINT-SIZED sources of light. As the path of rays from the star varies slightly, the apparent position fluctuates and the amount of starlight entering the eye flickers - the star sometimes appears brighter and sometimes fainter, which is the twinkling effect.

PLANETS do not twinkle: planets are much closer to the Earth and are seen as EXTENDED sources (a collection of a large number of point-sized sources). The total variation in the amount of light entering the eye from all these points averages out to zero, nullifying the twinkling effect.
ADVANCE SUNRISE AND DELAYED SUNSET:
Due to atmospheric refraction, the Sun is visible about 2 MINUTES BEFORE the actual sunrise and about 2 MINUTES AFTER the actual sunset.
"Actual sunrise" means the actual crossing of the horizon by the Sun.
The time difference between actual sunset and apparent sunset is about 2 minutes.
The apparent FLATTENING of the Sun's disc at sunrise and sunset is also due to atmospheric refraction.

items.question: What is atmospheric refraction?
items.answer: ATMOSPHERIC REFRACTION is the refraction (bending) of light by the Earth's atmosphere. It occurs because the physical conditions of the air (a medium of changing refractive index) are not stationary.

items.question: Why does the Sun appear before actual sunrise and after actual sunset?
items.answer: Due to ATMOSPHERIC REFRACTION, light from the Sun is bent by the atmosphere so the Sun appears raised above the horizon. Hence the Sun is visible about 2 minutes BEFORE actual sunrise and about 2 minutes AFTER actual sunset.

items.question: Why does a star appear slightly higher than its actual position when seen near the horizon?
items.answer: When starlight enters the Earth's atmosphere, it undergoes continuous refraction in a medium of gradually changing refractive index, and the atmosphere bends the starlight TOWARDS the normal. Because of this bending, the apparent position of the star is slightly raised, so the star appears HIGHER than its actual position when viewed near the horizon.

items.question: Why do stars twinkle?
items.answer: Stars twinkle due to ATMOSPHERIC REFRACTION of starlight. Stars are very distant and act as POINT-SIZED sources. As starlight passes through the atmosphere of continuously changing refractive index, its path varies slightly, so the apparent position of the star fluctuates and the amount of starlight entering the eye keeps changing. The star therefore appears brighter at some moments and fainter at others, producing the twinkling effect.

items.question: Why do planets not twinkle whereas stars do?
items.answer: PLANETS are much closer to the Earth and are seen as EXTENDED sources, i.e. a collection of a large number of point-sized sources of light. The variations in the amount of light coming from all these individual points AVERAGE OUT to zero, so there is no net flickering and planets do not twinkle. Stars, being very distant, behave as single point-sized sources whose light fluctuates, so they twinkle.

items.question: Explain the effects of atmospheric refraction with reference to twinkling of stars and advance sunrise/delayed sunset.
items.answer:
Atmospheric refraction is the bending of light by the non-stationary atmosphere.
(i) TWINKLING OF STARS: Starlight from a distant point-sized source is continuously refracted by the atmosphere of changing refractive index. The varying path causes the apparent position of the star and the amount of light entering the eye to fluctuate, making the star appear to twinkle. Planets, being extended sources, do not twinkle because the variations average out.
(ii) ADVANCE SUNRISE AND DELAYED SUNSET: Light from the Sun is bent by the atmosphere so the Sun's apparent position is above the horizon even when it is actually below it. Hence the Sun is seen about 2 minutes before actual sunrise and about 2 minutes after actual sunset. The flattening of the Sun's disc at sunrise and sunset is also due to atmospheric refraction.

items.question: What is scattering of light?
items.answer: SCATTERING OF LIGHT is the phenomenon in which light striking fine particles in a medium is reflected diffusely in different directions, making the path of light visible.

items.question: Name two natural phenomena caused by the scattering of light.
items.answer: Two phenomena caused by scattering of light are the BLUE COLOUR of the clear sky and the REDDENING of the Sun at sunrise and sunset (also the colour of deep sea water).

items.question: Why is the path of light visible through a colloidal solution but not through a true solution?
items.answer: In a TRUE solution the particles are extremely small and do not scatter light effectively, so the path of a beam of light is NOT visible. In a COLLOIDAL solution the particles are relatively LARGER and scatter the light, so the path of the light beam becomes VISIBLE.

items.question: On what does the colour of scattered light depend? Explain.
items.answer: The colour of scattered light depends on the SIZE of the scattering particles. Very FINE particles scatter mainly BLUE light (shorter wavelengths). Particles of LARGER size scatter light of longer wavelengths. If the scattering particles are LARGE enough, the scattered light may even appear WHITE.

items.question: Why are 'danger' signal lights made red in colour?
items.answer: 'Danger' signal lights are made RED because red light has the LONGEST wavelength among visible colours and is the LEAST scattered by fog or smoke. Because it is scattered the least, red light can travel through fog or smoke and be seen in the same colour even from a large distance, making it ideal for danger signals.

items.question: Explain scattering of light and how the size of particles affects the colour of scattered light, with examples.
items.answer:
SCATTERING OF LIGHT occurs when light strikes fine particles and is reflected diffusely in different directions, making the light's path visible. The colour of the scattered light depends on the SIZE of the scattering particles:
- Very fine particles scatter mainly BLUE (short-wavelength) light - this causes the blue colour of the sky.
- Larger particles scatter longer-wavelength light.
- Very large particles scatter all wavelengths, so the scattered light appears WHITE.
Examples: The clear sky appears blue because fine air molecules scatter blue light; danger signals are red because red light is least scattered and travels far; the Sun appears reddish at sunrise and sunset because most of the blue light is scattered away over the long path through the atmosphere.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The Earth's atmosphere is a heterogeneous mixture of minute particles, including smoke, tiny water droplets, suspended particles of dust, and molecules of air.

When a beam of light strikes such fine particles, the path of the beam becomes visible because the light reaches us after being reflected diffusely by these particles - this phenomenon gives rise to the TYNDALL EFFECT (studied in Class IX).
The Tyndall effect can be seen when a fine beam of sunlight enters a smoke-filled room through a small hole.
It can also be observed when sunlight passes through a canopy of a dense forest, where tiny water droplets in the mist scatter light.

The colour of the scattered light depends on the SIZE of the scattering particles: very fine particles scatter mainly BLUE light, while larger particles scatter light of LONGER wavelengths. If the particles are large enough, the scattered light may even appear WHITE.

items.question: What is the Tyndall effect?
items.answer: The TYNDALL EFFECT is the scattering of light by colloidal particles in the path of a light beam, which makes the path of the light VISIBLE.

items.question: Give two situations in which the Tyndall effect can be observed.
items.answer: The Tyndall effect can be observed (i) when a fine beam of sunlight enters a SMOKE-FILLED room through a small hole, and (ii) when sunlight passes through the CANOPY of a dense forest where tiny water droplets in the mist scatter light.

items.question: Why does the atmosphere produce the Tyndall effect?
items.answer: The Earth's atmosphere is a HETEROGENEOUS mixture of minute particles such as smoke, tiny water droplets, dust and air molecules. When a beam of light strikes these fine particles, it is reflected diffusely in different directions, making the path of the beam visible. This scattering of light by such particles is the TYNDALL EFFECT.

items.question: How does the size of particles affect the colour of light scattered in the Tyndall effect?
items.answer: In the Tyndall effect, the colour of the scattered light depends on the SIZE of the scattering particles. Very FINE particles scatter mainly BLUE (shorter-wavelength) light. Particles of LARGER size scatter light of longer wavelengths. If the scattering particles are LARGE enough, the scattered light may even appear WHITE, because all wavelengths are scattered almost equally.

items.question: Explain, with examples, how the Tyndall effect makes the path of light visible.
items.answer: When light passes through a medium containing fine suspended particles (a colloid), the particles scatter the light and reflect it diffusely towards our eyes, so we can see the path of the beam. For example, when a fine beam of sunlight enters a smoke-filled room through a small hole, the smoke particles scatter the light and the beam's path becomes visible. Similarly, sunlight passing through the mist in a dense forest canopy is scattered by tiny water droplets, again making its path visible.

items.question: Define the Tyndall effect, state the conditions for it, and explain the dependence of scattered-light colour on particle size.
items.answer:
The TYNDALL EFFECT is the scattering of light by colloidal particles, making the path of the light beam visible.
Conditions: The medium must contain fine suspended particles (such as smoke, dust, tiny water droplets or air molecules) larger than those in a true solution; the path of light is visible in a colloid but not in a true solution.
Dependence on particle size: Very fine particles scatter mainly blue light; larger particles scatter longer wavelengths; very large particles scatter all wavelengths so the scattered light appears white.
Examples: A beam of sunlight entering a smoke-filled room, and sunlight passing through the misty canopy of a dense forest, both show the Tyndall effect.

subtopics.subtopic_name: WHY IS THE COLOUR OF THE CLEAR SKY BLUE?

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The molecules of air and other fine particles in the atmosphere are SMALLER in size than the wavelength of visible light.
These small particles are more effective in scattering light of SHORTER wavelengths (blue end) than light of longer wavelengths (red end).
Red light has a wavelength about 1.8 TIMES greater than that of blue light.

When sunlight passes through the atmosphere, the fine particles scatter the BLUE colour (shorter wavelengths) more strongly than red; this scattered blue light enters our eyes, so the sky appears blue.
If the Earth had NO atmosphere, there would be no scattering, and the sky would have looked DARK.
The sky appears dark to passengers flying at very high altitudes, because scattering is not prominent at such heights.

items.question: Why does the clear sky appear blue?
items.answer: The fine air molecules in the atmosphere scatter the shorter-wavelength BLUE light of sunlight more strongly than red light. This scattered blue light enters our eyes, so the clear sky appears BLUE.

items.question: Why does the sky appear dark to an astronaut instead of blue?
items.answer: At very high altitudes (or in space) there is little or NO atmosphere to scatter sunlight. With no scattering of blue light, the sky appears DARK instead of blue to an astronaut.

items.question: How does the size of air molecules relate to the scattering of blue light?
items.answer: The air molecules and fine particles in the atmosphere are SMALLER than the wavelength of visible light. Such small particles are more effective at scattering SHORTER wavelengths, i.e. blue light, than longer-wavelength red light (red's wavelength is about 1.8 times that of blue). Hence blue light is scattered the most.

items.question: Explain why the sky would look dark if the Earth had no atmosphere.
items.answer: The blue colour of the sky is produced by the SCATTERING of sunlight by the fine particles of the atmosphere. If the Earth had NO atmosphere, there would be no particles to scatter the sunlight, so no scattered blue light would reach our eyes. As a result, the sky would appear DARK. This is why the sky looks dark to passengers flying at very high altitudes, where scattering is not prominent.

items.question: Why is blue light scattered more than red light by the atmosphere?
items.answer: The molecules of air and fine particles in the atmosphere are smaller than the wavelength of visible light, and such small particles scatter SHORTER wavelengths more effectively. Since BLUE light has a much shorter wavelength than RED light (red's wavelength is about 1.8 times greater than blue's), blue light is scattered much more strongly than red. This strongly scattered blue light reaching our eyes makes the sky appear blue.

items.question: Explain in detail why the clear sky appears blue and why it looks dark from very high altitudes.
items.answer:
The clear sky appears BLUE because of the scattering of sunlight by fine particles in the atmosphere. The air molecules are smaller than the wavelength of visible light, so they are more effective at scattering SHORTER wavelengths (blue) than longer wavelengths (red); red's wavelength is about 1.8 times that of blue. When sunlight passes through the atmosphere, the blue colour is scattered most strongly, and this scattered blue light entering our eyes makes the sky look blue.
At very high altitudes or in space, the atmosphere is very thin or absent, so there are few or no particles to scatter sunlight. With negligible scattering, no scattered blue light reaches the observer, and the sky appears DARK. This is why the sky looks dark to astronauts and to passengers flying at very high altitudes.

items.question: The human eye can focus on objects at different distances by adjusting the focal length of the eye lens. This is due to
items.answer:
(a) presbyopia.
(b) accommodation.
(c) near-sightedness.
(d) far-sightedness.
ANSWER: (b) accommodation.
EXPLANATION: Adjusting the focal length of the eye lens to focus on objects at different distances is the power of accommodation.

items.question: The human eye forms the image of an object at its
items.answer:
(a) cornea.
(b) iris.
(c) pupil.
(d) retina.
ANSWER: (d) retina.
EXPLANATION: The eye lens forms an inverted real image on the retina, the light-sensitive screen of the eye.

items.question: The least distance of distinct vision for a young adult with normal vision is about
items.answer:
(a) 25 m.
(b) 2.5 cm.
(c) 25 cm.
(d) 2.5 m.
ANSWER: (c) 25 cm.
EXPLANATION: For a normal young adult eye, the near point (least distance of distinct vision) is about 25 cm.

items.question: The change in focal length of an eye lens is caused by the action of the
items.answer:
(a) pupil.
(b) retina.
(c) ciliary muscles.
(d) iris.
ANSWER: (c) ciliary muscles.
EXPLANATION: The ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens, thereby changing its focal length (accommodation).

items.question: A person needs a lens of power -5.5 dioptres for correcting his distant vision. For correcting his near vision he needs a lens of power +1.5 dioptre. What is the focal length of the lens required for correcting (i) distant vision, and (ii) near vision?
items.answer:
ANSWER:
(i) For distant vision: P = -5.5 D, so f = 1/P = 1/(-5.5) = -0.18 m (approximately). The focal length for distant vision is about -0.18 m (concave lens).
(ii) For near vision: P = +1.5 D, so f = 1/P = 1/(1.5) = +0.67 m (approximately). The focal length for near vision is about +0.67 m (convex lens).

items.question: The far point of a myopic person is 80 cm in front of the eye. What is the nature and power of the lens required to correct the problem?
items.answer:
ANSWER:
For a myopic eye, a CONCAVE lens is required. The lens must form the image of an object at infinity at the far point (80 cm = 0.8 m).
So, object distance u = infinity and image distance v = -80 cm = -0.8 m.
Focal length f = v = -0.8 m (since for u = infinity, f = v).
Power P = 1/f = 1/(-0.8) = -1.25 D.
Nature: CONCAVE lens; Power = -1.25 D.

items.question: Make a diagram to show how hypermetropia is corrected. The near point of a hypermetropic eye is 1 m. What is the power of the lens required to correct this defect? Assume that the near point of the normal eye is 25 cm.
items.answer:
ANSWER:
A CONVEX lens is required to correct hypermetropia (refer to Figure 10.3(c): a converging lens placed before the eye forms the image of an object at 25 cm at the eye's near point of 1 m).
Object distance u = -25 cm = -0.25 m (normal near point); image distance v = -100 cm = -1 m (near point of the defective eye).
Using the lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f:
1/f = 1/(-1) - 1/(-0.25) = -1 + 4 = +3
So f = 1/3 m = +0.33 m, and Power P = 1/f = +3.0 D.
Nature: CONVEX lens; Power = +3.0 D.

items.question: Why is a normal eye not able to see clearly the objects placed closer than 25 cm?
items.answer: ANSWER: To see a nearby object clearly the eye lens must shorten its focal length by increasing its curvature. However, the focal length of the eye lens cannot be reduced below a certain minimum limit. For an object closer than 25 cm (the near point), the lens cannot decrease its focal length enough to form a sharp image on the retina, so the object appears blurred.

items.question: What happens to the image distance in the eye when we increase the distance of an object from the eye?
items.answer: ANSWER: When the distance of the object from the eye is increased, the image distance in the eye REMAINS PRACTICALLY THE SAME (constant), because the image is always formed on the retina at a fixed distance from the eye lens. The eye lens adjusts its focal length (accommodation) to keep the image focussed on the retina. (Textbook answer key: Yes - the image distance stays the same.)

items.question: Why do stars twinkle?
items.answer: ANSWER: Stars twinkle due to atmospheric refraction of starlight. Stars are very distant point-sized sources. As starlight passes through the atmosphere of continuously changing refractive index, its path varies slightly, so the apparent position of the star fluctuates and the amount of starlight entering the eye keeps changing - the star appears brighter at some moments and fainter at others, which is the twinkling effect.

items.question: Explain why the planets do not twinkle.
items.answer: ANSWER: Planets are much closer to the Earth and are seen as extended sources, i.e. a collection of a large number of point-sized sources of light. The total variation in the amount of light entering the eye from all these points averages out to zero, so there is no net flickering and the planets do not twinkle.

items.question: Why does the sky appear dark instead of blue to an astronaut?
items.answer: ANSWER: The blue colour of the sky is due to the scattering of sunlight by fine particles in the atmosphere. At the altitude of an astronaut (in space) there is little or no atmosphere, so there is no scattering of sunlight. With no scattered blue light reaching the eye, the sky appears dark instead of blue.
